Rêver au pluriel : la balle qui transcen: Dreaming in the Plural: The Ball That Transcends the Stadium
Des jeunes maghrébins qui ne se connaiss: Young Maghrebis who don’t know each other celebrate together in front of Café Timgad after Morocco’s loss to France. Photo: Djazia Bousnina
C’est l’Argentine qui a remporté la Coup: Argentina won the Qatar World Cup. But for many, it was the performance of the Moroccan team, which finished fourth, that transcended the soccer field.
Le mercredi 14 décembre 2022, les Maghré: On Wednesday, December 14, 2022, Montréal’s Maghrebis gather at Café Timgad to watch the World Cup semifinal between the Atlas Lions and Les Bleus. Morocco is the first Maghrebi, African and Muslim team to reach the semifinal of this prestigious tournament. We went there also to understand what this qualification means for Moroccans, Maghrebis and Africans in Montréal and Quebec.
Au Café Timgad, situé dans le Petit Magh: At Café Timgad, in Little Maghreb, the Morocco-France match is being broadcast. There, you discover how to dream, resist and celebrate, because any room with this much faith is a house of prayer. And any audience with this much spirit is a communion. Any soul with this much hope is a future. Morocco will not make it to the final of this World Cup; the Lions played the third-place match against Croatia, and lost. But beyond the standings, one thing is certain: being defeated so close to the goal only plants hope, which will germinate in the hearts of future generations.
À 13 h 30, la salle est pleine à craquer: At 1:30 p.m., the room is packed to the rafters; there are more than a hundred spectators. Although they are squeezed in like sardines, people keep arriving, because it turns out that “narrowness exists only in the heart,” as the owner of Café Timgad puts it, insisting loudly “[that] there’s still room for everyone.” As the drums resound, emotions rise in a great feeling of anticipation. History is being written with this decisive semifinal between Morocco and France.
Un groupe de jeunes hommes maghrébins ch: A group of young Maghrebi men sing and play music before the start of the match. Photo: Djazia Bousnina
« <l1>Hey yo, mabrouk 3lina, Hadi albida: “<l1>Hey yo, mabrouk 3lina, Hadi albidaya, mazal mazal</l1>” (Hey yo, congratulations to us, this is only the beginning, the best is yet to come), sings a group of young Algerian and Moroccan men, accompanying themselves with their drums, their <l2>tars</l2>, their <l3>derboukas</l3> and their <l4>qraqeb</l4>. Café Timgad is more than 8,000 km from <l5>the ancient Roman city</l5> that bears this name in Algeria. Yet within its four walls, you forget Montréal’s cold wind and are transported to the heart of the Maghreb by the songs, the warmth and the cacophony of Arabic-Amazigh dialects.
Hazzit Amar avec le drapeau d’Algerie au: Hazzit Amar with the Algerian flag at Café Timgad. Photo: Djazia Bousnina
En regardant la pièce bondée, Hazzit Ama: Looking at the packed room, Hazzit Amar declares proudly: “Morocco is my second country,” even though he has never lived in Morocco and has lived in Canada for about fifteen years. “Moroccans are my brothers. When our brothers are happy, that’s our joy,” explains the Algerian man, who is in his seventies. “They are the first of us to have climbed this obstacle, as Maghrebis, Africans and Muslims,” he says. “France colonized Algerians for 132 years. My mother fought in the war of liberation; in fact, I’m the nephew of Ali Khodja (an Algerian mujahid (fighter)). Even if French colonization was shorter in Morocco, playing against France is very political for all of us,” he adds, making a circular gesture to take in the whole café. “Moroccans helped us during the war of 1956-1962, and many Moroccans lost their lives there.” He closes his eyes and nods, recalling all the sacrifices, and continues: “They helped us in every way possible. The Tunisians too. We have to be grateful, and supporting Morocco in today’s battle is the least we can do.”
Plus que 10 minutes avant le début du ma: Ten minutes left before the start of the match, and the crowd chants: “God willing, God willing, Morocco is qualified. God willing, God willing, Morocco is qualified.” Hazzit stands up and exclaims: “Did you feel that? Don’t you feel it? All this hope! All this victory!” He turns to his compatriots with a smile on his lips: “I skipped work for this.” He’s not the only one. Mourad and his friends did too. “It’s a source of pride, being Moroccan. We’re truly proud of our team, of the players’ efforts and of the importance of what they’ve accomplished.” Tar in hand, he starts to play, then adds: “We beat Spain, we beat Portugal; so we can beat France – one colonizer at a time!” he exclaims before playing again. The café lights dim, signalling the start of the match. Hands on hearts, the spectators sing the Moroccan national anthem: “Your champion has risen/And answered your call/And in my mouth/And in my blood/Your love has shaken light and embers/My brothers, let us go/Toward what is highest.”
Mourad et ses amisi jouent le tar au caf: Mourad and his friends play the tar at Café Timgad. Photo: Djazia Bousnina
<strong>« Ils ne savent pas qu’on croit: “They don’t know we believe in them”
Cinq minutes après le coup d’envoi, Théo: Five minutes after kickoff, Théo Hernandez scores a destabilizing goal against Morocco. In response, Idir, a young Algerian, starts playing the derbouka, and the room immediately chants: “Mazel, mazel maghrib, mazel,” which means both that the best is yet to come and that Morocco is still here, standing tall. Time passes, and the Atlas Lions’ missed chances breed frustration. Idir, faithful to his post, wants to ease people’s nerves with his music. “We’re here for the atmosphere, but above all, we’re here to absorb the stress and send back positive vibes,” confides the young taxi driver, who also took time off for the occasion. “The players are agitated because of the pressure of the match” is a sentence repeated by many throughout the first half. A young man standing, head tilted up as he watches the television, even wonders: “Why are they so stressed? Don’t they know we believe in them and support them, no matter the result?”
Ce sentiment est partagé par Niama, qui: Niama shares this feeling, clapping to the rhythm of the music in support of her national team. “Me, I’m proud of them. I hope they’ll be able to score in the second half, but if not, it’s okay, I’m still proud of them,” she says. “Besides, I came here today to celebrate them. I called work to say I was sick, because a day like this, you live it as a community. And the result of the match won’t change my support for them.”
Hélas, alors que l’horloge indique 15 h: Alas, as the clock strikes 3:37 p.m., Randal Kolo Muani scores a second goal for France. Morocco, which had conceded only one goal in its five previous matches, has let in two in this one. With less than 10 minutes of play left, spectators leave Café Timgad. People walk out, some frustrated and heartbroken, others drained, needing a break after this emotional roller coaster. Those who stay until the end warmly applaud the Atlas Lions’ performance. Young women are in tears, a son comforts his father, who hides his face in his hands – Morocco will not make it to the final.
Pourtant, lorsqu’on sort rue Jean-Talon,: Yet when you step out onto Jean-Talon Street, you find people of all ages waving their flags, singing and dancing. Despite this defeat, “they won the hearts of many people, and just reaching the semifinal is a great achievement for the African continent and the Arab world; it’s something we can be very proud of,” says Sadeen Salah, speaking of a victory all the same. “Filistin Shuhada, Filistin Shuhada, Filistin” (Palestine, the martyrs, Palestine, the martyrs, Palestine) was repeated by all the revellers. A Palestinian herself, Sadeen tells us that the Moroccan team and its supporters showed great solidarity with the Palestinian cause. “There was a lot of support for Palestinians, even though we weren’t in the World Cup. It was very moving for us; it shows we haven’t been forgotten. For me, when Morocco plays, it’s my country playing.”
Ce sentiment d’appartenance et de représ: This sense of belonging and representation is strongly felt among young people from immigrant backgrounds. Dania Zaron holds up her flag, which unites many Arab countries. “My sisters and I were born in France, so we’re supposed to support France, but we’re of Egyptian and Tunisian origin. Our ancestors are Arab and Maghrebi; without a doubt we support Morocco, even in defeat,” says the international economics student.
Diana Zaron qui partage son drapeau avec: Diana Zaron sharing her flag with a young Algerian. Photo: Djazia Bousnina
« Appuyer le Maroc signifiait appuyer l’: “Supporting Morocco meant supporting the underdog, supporting people like us, who aren’t going to bring the victory home to a Western country that will exploit them even more,” says Hiba. This young Moroccan woman explains that, for her compatriots, these celebrations are “a kind of cure.” “Singing the same songs, reciting the same slogans we saw our parents recite, it brings us a little bit of Morocco here in Montréal.” The excitement surrounding Morocco’s victories during the World Cup is prompting many young people to discover the atmosphere of the Maghrebi neighbourhood. For many of them, it was a first. “We don’t really have opportunities here to be in community. It’s rare for our communities to be together, and not to hold a demonstration against Legault, but simply to appreciate and enjoy this achievement,” says Hiba of the diaspora.
D’une part, cette Coupe du monde a permi: On the one hand, this World Cup made it possible to confront Africa’s colonial past through several matches, notably against Belgium, Spain, Portugal and France. “A wave of decolonization is sweeping over questions of how the Orient is perceived. Also, for many dual nationals, we are finally and fully reclaiming our Africanness, our indigeneity and our Islam,” says Hiba, hand on her chest. “It’s a result of decolonizing the self, of breaking the colonial prism in which our identity was conceived. Like our team, we are diverse, we are not a monolith. The Moroccan presence is in itself a form of resistance. Except for Moroccans, nobody expected us to get that far,” she adds proudly.
D’autre part, il y a cette détermination: On the other hand, there is this determination and perseverance in highlighting present-day injustice. “The countries we played against have a significant Moroccan diaspora as well as other marginalized groups. They often experience racism and different types of discrimination. So, by being represented, we felt strengthened, seen and capable of facing anything,” concludes Hiba.
Le vent montréalais siffle, les drapeaux: The Montréal wind whistles, flags flutter in the air, young people claim a future in which they are winners. From their cars, on their horses, police officers watch them celebrate this unprecedented victory. Here, in front of Café Timgad, we learn to be, we learn to dream.
